2bbb/fm1-firmware-collection.summary: Not a firmware: a catalog of community FM-1 firmwares, holding 375 of them as git submodules pinned to their upstream heads, with Python scripts and CI workflows that build the ones that publish no package of their own. It makes no sound itself.

findings.text: It is a collection of other firmwares: every firmware's code is in a git submodule under firmwares/<owner>/<repo>, and its own code is only the cataloguing and build scripts and workflows (MIT). Each firmware keeps its own licence.
Its README says firmwares without a licence file are listed and pinned but never built or redistributed, and that its CI builds are untested on hardware.
The scan's code matches (Plaits, msfa, reSID, STK and others) and AI mentions all come from the submodules' own trees and branch names, not from this repository's files.
findings.evidence: brief: every match is [submodule ...], 0 own; .gitmodules branch names such as codex/... and claude/...

findings.text: Its documents mention Claude, Codex.

2bbb/fm1-firmware-collection.hardware_note: none (a collection of other firmwares, not a firmware)

devrvega/crt-4.summary: CRT-4 is a four-track groovebox that plays the sound chips of nine game consoles and home computers (Atari 2600, C64, NES, PC Engine, Genesis, Game Boy, SNES, PlayStation, N64), each with two drum kits, sixteen sounds, its own effects and an animated scene. Its chip engines are its own code written from the chips' public documentation, and its samples are synthesized by a generator in the source; its frame comes from the author's LCD-4 and IND-1, built on AMB-1.

findings.text: Its LICENSING.md says the chip engines follow the chips' public documentation and contain no code, firmware, ROM contents or data of the consoles' makers, and that tables such as the S-DSP's Gaussian interpolation are computed by CRT-4 itself.

It keeps a script, inherited through its bases from AMB-1, that packages its emulator as a claude.ai Artifact, and its .gitignore excludes .serena/ and docs/superpowers/ (AI coding-agent folders); there are no AI tool files at its top level.
It is the base of the same author's BOP-1.
Its LICENSING.md says it never enables the FM-1's Bluetooth / Wi-Fi radio.

Its engine is its own, built on Charles Vestal's AMB-1.

findings.text: CLAUDE.md at its top level holds the project's working rules for an AI agent, and CONTRIBUTING.md welcomes AI-assisted contributions.
Its documents describe having any language model (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or a local one) write a LAB sound from a few words, using instructions SIDOU publishes, and loading it onto the device.
Its firmware is C; its host tools, tests and table generator are a Rust workspace, and REUSE lint runs in CI so every file carries a licence label.

dspaudio/mc-1.summary: MC-1 is a four-part groovebox inspired by Roland's MC-303 and LA synthesis: three melodic parts and a sixteen-lane drum part, with 112 LA-PCM sounds (recorded attacks from CC0 instrument recordings joined to synthesized harmonic sustain), 16 303-style Acid sounds, eight synthesized drum kits and shared reverb, delay and chorus banks, spread over both of the FM-1's cores. Its engine, effects, sequencer and UI are its own fixed-point code on a platform taken from the author's ORBIT firmware (from SLOOP and Felucca).

It includes FM-1 SID (joakimeriksson/fm1-sid) as a submodule: a GPL-3.0 SID synth and C64 tune player firmware on Felucca/Dinghy, with GoatTracker 2's player (GPL-2.0-or-later) and a prebuilt sidplayer.fwsc; reSID 0.16 is fetched at build time, not held.
Its technical report says the work was done by one person directing an AI coding agent (Claude Code); its work log PLAN.md records Claude reviews.

Its README credits the community's reverse engineering (AL-255/FM-1-RE, ip2k/lunar-modulator, kagaimiq's jielie) and Felucca's hardware layer as references, and says no GPL code is in the repository itself.

The Braids MACRO engine and the ADPCM engine are opt-in build profiles; the standard build and hosted demo leave them out, and its README says the full MACRO recipe currently exceeds flash capacity.
It has experimental build targets for M-VAVE's SMK-37 Pro, Elite and MKE-P37 keyboards, and an optional second-core worker that is off by default.

Its UI font, M8Stealth (CC BY-SA 3.0), is compiled into the GPL-3.0-only firmware; LICENSING.md keeps the font data under its own terms. CC BY-SA 3.0 is not among the licences the FSF lists as GPL-compatible.

findings.text: It makes no sound of its own: it is a USB audio interface, Bluetooth audio receiver and master EQ/limiter, with no synth engine.
It runs on both cores: the second core decodes the Bluetooth audio codecs and resamples, with no single-core fallback. It uses its own Bluetooth stack rather than JieLi's binary libraries.
It is installed through m-bootloader: its README asks to flash m-bootloader with M-Flasher first, and its packages bundle the m-bootloader binary.
The repository is MPL-2.0, but its aptX decoder (libfreeaptx) is LGPL-2.1-or-later and several codecs are Apache-2.0; LICENSING.md lists each part with its licence file.
AGENTS.md at its top level and AI agent skills in .agents/skills/ (copied from maxfridbe/mvave-fm1); the vendored fm1-base documents mention a Claude skill.

findings.text: The code is GPL-3.0-only, but the firmware embeds the singer's pixel art, which is Hatsune Miku fan art under Crypton's Piapro Character License: free and non-commercial only and not relicensable; LICENSING.md says so and explains how to replace it.
Claude Code handoff and review files (CLAUDE_HANDOFF.md, CLAUDE_CODE_REVIEW.md) are at its top level, and its notices say the singer art and the demo song's lyrics were made with ChatGPT.

It builds on Dinghy's platform rather than holding a copy: its build clones Dinghy at a pinned commit, patches it and swaps in Miku-FM's own application, which is why the scan finds no base code in the repository. Its song slots and settings sector are those other Felucca-family firmwares use, so saving replaces their data.
The scan's partial matches with msfa / Dexed (29%) and Yarns (43%) are its credited Apache-2.0 MSFA port and its own generated sine tables.

findings.text: Its licence is GPL-3.0-only with an FM1 linking exception (hence GitHub's NOASSERTION), and it links M-VAVE's proprietary binary engine library, libfm1_engine.a, whose source is not supplied; all of this is fm1_open's own arrangement.

It carries M-VAVE's original V15 firmware image so the browser installer can return the FM-1 to stock; user presets live in the last 64 KB of the sample area, so the first SAVE overwrites the end of the sample bank.
The scan's partial matches of web/synth/dx7pitchenv.c with msfa and Dexed (about 40%) are fm1_open's credited Apache-2.0 port of msfa, not GPL Dexed code.
Every riff it plays is checked against fingerprints of the 7-note figures in its reference recordings and changed if it would repeat one.
The only AI trace is an ignored Codex working folder (.codex-sinco/) in its .gitignore, inherited from fm1_open.

zvenson/zp12.summary: zp12 is a 12-bit sampling drum machine in the spirit of the 1980s SP-12 / SP-1200: 32 pads of packed 12-bit samples at 26.04 or 27.5 kHz, pitched without interpolation, eight output channels (two with a resonant SSM2044-style filter), a loop sequencer and sampling over USB or in the browser. The sampler engine and sequencer are its own; the platform and send effects come from SLOOP, Felucca and sloopDX.

findings.text: CLAUDE.md, a project brief for Claude sessions, is at its top level.
Its saved state lives in a flash area that sloopDX leaves free but stock SLOOP uses for its own samples; the README says to back those up before installing.
The same sampler engine also builds natively for another device, the VIBE FM, from vibe/.
